---
applyTo: "app/services/**/*.rb,app/forms/**/*.rb,app/controllers/**/*.rb,app/jobs/**/*.rb,lib/**/*.rb"
---

# Services

- Put service objects in `app/services/`, e.g. `NewsletterClient` in `app/services/newsletter_client.rb`.
- You MUST NOT give a service object a `call` method. Name each public method after what it does, e.g. `NewsletterClient#create_newsletter` and `NewsletterClient#deliver`.
- Call a service from an action, not from a form or controller, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new.create_newsletter(post)` in `Posts::SendNewsletter#call`. Forms, controllers and jobs call the action. A form or controller MAY call a service directly only to read a value when nothing changes, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new.fetch_stats(post.newsletter_id)` in a controller. A controller reads the value before the view renders, following the controllers instructions. A job MAY call a service directly only when it is the only place that does the task, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new.deliver(post)` in `NotifySubscribersJob`. Move the call into an action when a second caller needs it.
- Build a request body in the service, from the records passed to it, e.g. `NewsletterClient#create_newsletter(post)`. You MUST NOT make a service method take a request built by its caller, e.g. `create_newsletter(request)`. Pass a value the service can't read from the record as a keyword argument.
- Build a service's request body as a hash. When it takes more than a line, build it in a private method on the service named after what it builds, e.g. `NewsletterClient#newsletter_body(post)`, not in a class in `app/models/`. A class the app uses for its own work stays with the rest of the app's code, e.g. in `app/models/` or `app/serializers/`. You SHOULD NOT define a `Data` object for the body in a service without a gateway.
- Read a service's settings from a `Rails.application.config.x` namespace named after the service, e.g. `config.x.newsletter_client.api_key`. Set the values in one place, e.g. `config/application.rb`, from credentials or `ENV`. You MUST NOT read `Rails.application.credentials` or `ENV` in a service, and you MUST NOT put a setting straight on `config.x`, e.g. `config.x.newsletter_client_api_key`.
- Take each setting as a keyword argument to `initialize`, with the setting as its default, e.g. `def initialize(api_key: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.api_key!)`. Read required settings with a bang, e.g. `api_key!`, so a missing or blank value raises a `KeyError`. You MUST NOT pass the settings from app code, e.g. `NewsletterClient.new`, not `NewsletterClient.new(api_key: ...)`. Only specs pass them, e.g. `described_class.new(api_key: "test-key")`.
- When the app can run without a service, give the service a `configured?` class method that checks its required settings without the bang, e.g. `config.api_key.present? && config.base_url.present?` on `Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client`. Check it before building the service in code that can skip the work, e.g. `return unless NewsletterClient.configured?` in `NotifySubscribersJob#perform`. You MUST NOT add a separate `enabled` setting, and you MUST NOT rescue `KeyError` to find out whether a service is set up.
- When a service's settings are saved on a record, build it with a class method on the service that passes the record's settings to `new`, named `for` or `for_<source>`, e.g. `for_integration`. For example, `def self.for(integration) = new(api_key: integration.api_key, base_url: integration.base_url)` on `NewsletterClient`. Make those settings required keywords with no default, and leave app-wide settings to their `config.x` defaults, e.g. `api_path: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.api_path!`. You MUST NOT add a method to the record that builds the service, e.g. `integration.client`.
- When a service keeps connections open to another service, borrow them from a `ConnectionPool` kept on the service in a private `Concurrent::Map` constant and keyed on the connection settings, e.g. `POOLS.compute_if_absent({ base_url: })` in `NewsletterClient.pool_for(base_url:)`. Take the pool as a required first argument to `initialize`, e.g. `def initialize(pool, api_key:)`, and borrow from it in each method, e.g. `pool.with { |connection| ... }`. Build the service with a class method that finds the pool: `NewsletterClient.default` when every setting comes from `config.x`, e.g. `new(pool_for(base_url: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.base_url!), api_key: Rails.application.config.x.newsletter_client.api_key!)`, or `NewsletterClient.for(integration)` (or `for_integration`) when the settings come from a record, e.g. `new(pool_for(base_url: integration.base_url), api_key: integration.api_key)`. Pass connection settings only to `pool_for`, and keep `pool_for` private. You MUST NOT pass a pool to `new` from outside the service. Only specs and the service's own class methods pass one. You MUST NOT let a pooled connection carry one set of credentials to a service built with another. Send credentials with each request, e.g. an `Authorization` header, or include them in the pool's key. See https://bmorrall.github.io/happy_rails/patterns/connection-pools/.
- TODO: Which kinds of service objects to write.
- Give each service its own errors: an `Error < StandardError` class inside the service, and a subclass for each failure a caller handles on its own, e.g. `NewsletterClient::UnprocessableError < Error`. Rescue the HTTP library's errors in the service and raise the service's error, e.g. `rescue Faraday::Error => e` then `raise Error.new(e.message, ...)`. You MUST NOT let a library's error escape a service.
- Give a service's error the details of the failed call as keywords, e.g. `http_method:`, `url:`, `status:` and `body:` on `NewsletterClient::Error`.
- Make HTTP calls in the service until it gets too big to read. Then move the code that talks to the other service's API into a gateway in `lib/`, e.g. `NewsletterGateway` in `lib/newsletter_gateway.rb`. The service keeps taking records and building requests, and calls the gateway, e.g. `@gateway.create_newsletter(request)`. The private method that built the body then builds the gateway's request.
- Write a gateway in plain Ruby that takes and returns plain values, e.g. strings, arrays and hashes, and takes the request its service built, e.g. `NewsletterGateway#create_newsletter(request)`. You MUST NOT use Rails in a gateway, e.g. `Rails.application.config`, `Rails.logger`, credentials or `ENV`, and you MUST NOT pass it records.
- A gateway MAY take and return `Data` objects that it defines at its top, e.g. `CreateNewsletterRequest = Data.define(:title, :body, :visibility)` and `Newsletter = Data.define(:id, :status)` in `NewsletterGateway`. Name a request after the gateway method that takes it, e.g. `CreateNewsletterRequest` for `create_newsletter`, not after the service method that builds it, because several service methods can call one gateway method, e.g. `NewsletterClient#create_public_newsletter` and `NewsletterClient#create_private_newsletter`. Name a reply after what it holds, e.g. `Newsletter`. The service builds the request, e.g. `request = NewsletterGateway::CreateNewsletterRequest.new(title: post.title, body: post.body, visibility: "public")` then `@gateway.create_newsletter(request)`, and the gateway turns it into the body it sends. You MUST NOT use a `Struct` for them.
- When a gateway's reply holds more than the resource, e.g. a cursor for the next page or the call's request ID, return a response `Data` object named after the method that holds the resources and the extra values, e.g. `FetchAllStatsResponse = Data.define(:stats, :next_cursor)` for `fetch_all_stats`. Keep each resource in its own object, e.g. `NewsletterStats`.
- Take each gateway setting as a keyword argument to `initialize` with no default, e.g. `def initialize(api_key:, base_url:, api_path:)`. Read the settings from `config.x` in the service, and pass them to the gateway, e.g. `NewsletterGateway.new(api_key:, base_url:, api_path:)` in `NewsletterClient#initialize`.
- Write one gateway for each outside API, and share it between the services that use that API.
- Give a gateway its own errors with the details of the failed call, e.g. `NewsletterGateway::Error`. Rescue them in the service, and raise the service's own errors with the same details.
